The short version

I’m a student at Greenfield School in Ecopark, Hưng Yên, with a real passion for business. At home I’m the eldest of four kids, which made me a leader, a teacher and the go-to babysitter long before I had any official title.

I’m easygoing, cheerful and full of energy. My strengths are creativity and leadership, and I would always rather try something and learn from it than only read about it.

When I’m not working on a project, I’m drawing, playing sports, listening to music, at the gym or cooking. And I really, really don’t like onions.

Why business?

Three reasons, in my own words.

It’s in my blood

Both my parents are businesspeople, and I’ve picked up something from each of them. But it isn’t only something I inherited: business genuinely excites me.

It fits my skills

I’ve found that I have some of what business needs. I can lead and bring people with me, I communicate well, I’m creative, and I care deeply about the work.

It leads to my dream

Business is the road to the dream I’m working toward: founding the biggest milk tea brand in Asia.

Summer 2024, Hải Dương

Mr.Bas, my summer café

Summer 2024 gave me two months off, and one of them was already booked for a camp in New Zealand. So I set myself a one-month challenge: earn at least 4 million VND on my own, and learn real business skills along the way.

I noticed that staff at the Hải Dương office of YODY, the fashion company my parents founded, bought snacks and drinks all day long. So I wrote a business plan for a small food and drink counter.

Yes, it was my parents’ company. I still had to get my plan approved, rent a small space next to the canteen and win customers one cup at a time.

  1. Before day 1

    Ask first

    I surveyed the office. Milk tea and coffee were the top picks, so that’s where we started.

  2. Before day 1

    Build a supply chain

    I searched for every drink-ingredient supplier I could find, chose one for bulk orders, found an ice supplier, and kept the ice from melting by borrowing space in the canteen fridge.

  3. Days 1 to 3

    Sold out

    Nobody knew Mr.Bas, and people were loyal to big chains like Highlands Coffee. So I gave away free drinks first, let word of mouth do its job and put posters all over the office. Orders poured in. Some customers waited 20 minutes for a cup.

  4. Day 4

    Sales crash

    Orders suddenly dropped. The quality hadn’t changed; people were simply bored of a two-item menu. I added tropical fruit tea, made with fruit I bought at the market, and red plum juice, then promoted them in the company’s Gapo Work groups with my dad’s permission. The customers came back.

  5. After that

    Customers choose the menu

    Google Forms let customers vote on what we made next, and comments like “less sugar” went straight into the recipes. When they asked for food, I swapped our slowest drinks for tofu pudding and cookies. By week three we had changed the menu about ten times, but never the milk tea and coffee that sold every single week.

  6. Week 4

    Our best seller

    We launched a mixed yogurt cup, half snack and half drink. It became our hottest item and had its biggest day at the end of that week.

The team, and how we ran it

My little sister brought in customers, Sun made drinks with me and kept the books, Pan handled deliveries, and my best friend Bảo An joined me behind the counter. Every week we reviewed what worked and what didn’t, planned the next week, and I paid wages based on each person’s role and results. Sun’s records were accurate to the last đồng, so we always knew what was selling and what was fading.

Leftover cookies went to the cleaners and security guards. Not as marketing, just as respect.

Before Mr.Bas, business was theory I thought I’d only need in a few years. After it, money stopped being the main goal. The lessons were the real profit.

May 2024, Hanoi. 3rd Prize

Asian Business Simulation

ABS is a competition where teams run a simulated company. I was placed with seven strangers from across Vietnam, four boys and four girls, and we named our team SEB.

On our first call I ran for team leader against Hà, a year older than me and with a seriously impressive track record. I lost the debate and became vice-leader, covering technology, finance and product. I’d had a head start, because my parents paid for business classes before the competition, so I taught those lessons back to the team. We added a low-cost business course and a shared study plan so everyone was ready.

  1. Auction

    We bid for machines and materials and won a wood machine. A house needs 1 steel, 2 bricks and 3 wood, so we bargained hard for steel and bricks. We built one house: enough to get through, not our best result.

  2. Operation, worth 50% of the score

    Two teammates ran our simulated company while the rest of us prepared the final pitch. Honestly, it didn’t go as well as we hoped.

  3. Pitching, over two days

    The first brief was high-tech furniture. My idea was the Naturalize Desk: a three-tier desk with a rainwater collection system, built-in plants and fertilizer. The second brief arrived the night before, so we built the slides overnight and an A0 design board the next morning.

Plot twist

On day two my charger broke, my phone died and my alarm never rang. The guesthouse owner knocked on my door after my mom called him. Then the driver took me to the wrong Phenikaa campus, 10 km away. I still made it.

Result: SEB placed 3rd in ABS Vietnam, which earned us a spot in the next round in China. I couldn’t go, because I was already booked for summer camp in New Zealand. What I took home: persistence, creativity and logical thinking under pressure. Also, always pack a spare charger.

Thailand, 2024

Should this store stay open?

In 2024 I travelled to Thailand with my family, half holiday and half work. My parents’ company had opened a small store in an older shopping mall near the edge of the city, and Dad asked us kids to look around and find what wasn’t working.

I walked the whole mall first. Then, on the way to lunch, Dad asked me one question.

My takeaway: great design can’t save the wrong location. Start with who your customer is, then decide where to be.

Dad

If you were me, what would you do with this store?

Me

I’d close it.

The store looks great: clean, tidy, nicely designed. But the location doesn’t work.

This mall is old. Almost every shopper here is between 50 and 80, and our customers are 20 to 40.

Dad

You’re right.

And then we had a very big lunch.

Leading, and sometimes losing

Big brother of three

I became a leader before I could spell the word. Each time a new sibling arrived, I learned to share my time, take responsibility and be an example worth copying. When our parents were out, I looked after everyone, taught them what I’d learned and helped them through hard moments. Fun fact: I picked the name Pan for the third of us, after Peter Pan.

Team leader at 12

Led a 30-person team, 15 boys and 15 girls, at the Superior Teens camp. We won 3rd prize.

Vice-leader at ABS

Lost the leader debate, then taught the whole team what I knew.

Green House captain elections

Greenfield’s 2,000 students are split into five Houses that battle in the school Olympics, very Harry Potter. I ran for captain of the Green House twice. My pitch: when a team wins, everyone wins together, and a captain listens to every member.

2Campaigns
0Wins

What went wrong

I practised a lot. I trained myself to speak on stage in front of thousands of students and recorded hundreds of videos of myself talking to my phone. I thought I was confident. My campaign video was polished, with careful editing and the right music, and my profile looked good. Only the speech was left.

But the moment I stepped on stage, the pressure of facing thousands of students and teachers felt completely different from every rehearsal and every project presentation I’d done. My mind went blank. I kept it short, and I spoke without the conviction I’d planned.

I made the same mistake both times. There’s still a wall I need to get past: a psychological one, somewhere deep inside.

Nine stories with my dad. Here are four.

2013, age 3

Climbed to Bàn Cờ Tiên peak and back, about 3 km of mountain trail, without being carried once.

Set a clear goal. Rest when you’re tired. Don’t quit.

2015, age 5

Learning to ride a bike, I fell ten times in one practice. Every time, I stood up, shouted “Yes!” and rode on.

Every fall teaches you something. Learn to get up on your own.

2016

Dad gave Sun and me 14,000 VND for ice cream that cost more. On our third try, we came back with ice cream and the money: the seller gave it to us for free.

You’ll never have “enough” to start. Ask, try another way, keep going.

2017

I broke Dad’s expensive phone and didn’t tell the truth at first. He told me no phone is worth more than my character.

Own your mistakes.

Where I’m headed

When I was seven, my dad asked how I’d earn money. I said: by making people happy. Ten years later, that’s still the plan.

Next stop: studying business at university, starting in 2027. After that: founding the biggest milk tea brand in Asia, one happy customer at a time.
